title: Cloud endpoint cost + latency signal playbook
content:
Purpose:
Quick-source playbook for field sellers and solution engineers to surface operational signals (cost/latency/availability) vs public cloud managed endpoints and use those signals to position Redwood. Focused on pragmatic examples, short sales lines, and tests we can run in-house to validate claims.

TL;DR (one-paragraph):
Cloud vendors offer convenient managed endpoints but hide key operational tradeoffs: coarse batching controls, limited KV/prefix cache, unclear tail-latency under burst, and opaque cost-for-latency math across GPU types. Redwood's messaging: predictable latency and observable economics — you can optimize per-route cost with aggressive caching, fine-grained batching, and model-variant fallback without rebuilding infra. For customers who run LLM features in production, that translates to lower unit cost and fewer user-facing latency incidents.

Quick use-case signals to listen for (how buyers describe problems):
- "We see big token spikes at peak usage and our latency jumps" => ask about burst protection and fallbacks.
- "Cloud bills are unpredictable month-to-month" => ask how they're tracking per-route/token costs and what controls they have.
- "Our compliance team needs private networking + KMS" => probe VPC/HSM + audit log needs.
- "Dev teams are re-implementing caching/queuing" => surface our managed cache/batching.

Signal matrix (field-friendly cheat sheet):
- Cost transparency: Cloud vendors: per-instance/hour + opaque GPU-type multipliers; often charge for idle or provisioning time. Redwood: per-token + per-embedding unit (hosted) or predictable reserved capacity (Dedicated) + clear per-route cost breakdowns in Console.
- Tail latency during bursts: Cloud vendors: autoscale lag and cold-startish behavior on managed endpoints (esp. multi-tenant); limited visibility into queuing. Redwood: pre-warmed pools, burst capacity tiers and canary fallbacks to cheaper model variants.
- Batching & KV cache control: Cloud vendors: limited batching knobs or hidden infra-level batching; KV caching is customer-implemented. Redwood: workload-aware batching suggestions, automatic KV/prefix caching, and runtime-level cache controls.
- Private deployments & compliance: Cloud vendors: VPC/private endpoints possible but with multi-account networking complexity; variable KMS integrations. Redwood: private control plane + on-prem option with HSM support and integrated audit logs.
- Observability: Cloud vendors: metrics at endpoint/instance level; limited token-level cost attribution. Redwood: token-level cost/latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards, eval/regression hooks.

Field-friendly win themes (short):
- "Predictable unit economics": Show how we reduce tokens by caching + batching and surface exact $/route.
- "Latency you can SLAs for": Demonstrate deterministic SLOs with pre-warmed pools + fallbacks.
- "Drop-in ops for infra teams": Same API across hosted/dedicated/private so platform teams avoid building bespoke wrappers.
- "Operational regressions catchable before they hit users": tie evals/prompt sets to rollouts and regression alerts.

Example one-liners for outreach or pitch decks:
- "You don’t have to choose between low latency and low cost — Redwood optimizes both at serving time."
- "Keep dev velocity and get infra-level performance controls without hiring an inference team."
- "Predictable bills: per-route visibility lets you stop guessing which feature cost you money."

Suggested playbook flow for SEs during discovery call:
1) Ask for monthly token/embedding spend and top 3 high-throughput routes.
2) Ask about tail-latency incidents in past 90 days and what was done (retries, user-facing errors).
3) Ask whether they’ve implemented prefix caching or batching and who owns it.
4) Offer a lightweight benchmark: 30m synthetic burst test + latency and bill delta estimation.

Proof points & micro-benchmarks we should surface/do: (quick notes, we need engineering to run a few)
- 1M token/day route with and without prefix cache: show % token reduction and delta $/month.
- 300 concurrent short-chat sessions (seq len ~64): measure p50/p95/p99 on GCP/Azure managed endpoints vs Redwood-hosted with same model variant and compute.
- Cold-surge test: ramp 0->200 qps in 60s and measure latency spike and error rate across providers and our dedicated pools.
- Cost-per-token breakdown: unbundle infra-hour vs per-token economics on each vendor and model.

Objections likely from procurement/infra and suggested rebuttals:
- Proc: "Cloud vendor is already enterprise-approved and cheaper via committed discounts."
  - Rebuttal: "Committed discounts fix part of the cost but they don’t buy you per-route economics or caching. We reduce raw token consumption and give you exact per-feature cost to compare to committed pricing — often yielding lower effective cost for high-throughput features."
- Infra: "We prefer one cloud provider for consolidated billing/ops."
  - Rebuttal: "We integrate with your cloud and can run Dedicated or Private inside your VPC — preserves consolidated ops while giving you inference controls not available in managed endpoints."
- Engineers: "We can build this ourselves on managed instances."
  - Rebuttal: "You can, but it’s a multi-quarter eng investment to reach production-grade batching, KV cache, autoscaling, and observability. We provide a tested runtime and rollouts with fewer ops overhead and measurable unit-economics improvements."

Sales attachments to create (TODOs):
- Short 1-pager: "Cost vs Latency: What vendors don’t tell you" (include a simple chart and one benchmark).
- One-slide battle card for AWS/GCP/Azure each (bullets: ops risk, hidden cost, where they win).
- Quick benchmark kit: scripts and instructions for 3 micro-benchmarks above + expected output templates.

Language framing to avoid:
- Avoid using vague absolutes: "always" or "never" when talking about vendor behavior. Use "often" and "commonly observed".
- Avoid implying vendor security/compliance deficits. Instead, frame as "operational tradeoffs" and highlight Redwood’s options (Private, KMS/HSM).

Open questions (research/eng required):
- How much does AWS SageMaker Serverless endpoint cold-start behavior vary across instance families in our internal tests? (ask infra bench team)
- Can we produce a reproducible GCP-managed batching workload to isolate vendor-level batching vs our batching?
- What are limits/gaps in Azure OpenAI managed endpoint region coverage for customers in EU + APAC?

Next steps & owners:
- Run the 3 micro-benchmarks internally (owner: eng-applied-ml, lead: Ethan Chu).
- Draft 1-pager and three vendor battle slides (owner: go-to-market content, lead: Priya Shah).
- Build benchmark kit repo and link in this doc (owner: solutions-engineering, lead: Liam O'Connor).

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep this doc light-weight — primary deliverables: 1-pager + scripts.
- We should avoid rehashing generic "feature parity" claims; stick to measurable operational signals.
- Put a short annotated example of a customer's cost-savings story once we have benchmark numbers.

End.
